label: SJ
reason_kind: change to the definition of correct
reasoning: The accepted work was narrowly scoped: make the grader fail a run that names an act where none was expected. That narrow slice is delivered and its own unit test passes -- in isolation an ordinary delivered result under 'A shown result closes the work.' But the same branch of code also governs a second, unrequested case whose correct behaviour is already written down in the eval's own cost model (print a note, not a failure), and the delivered code now fails that case too, turning 4 previously-correct runs red. Nobody asked for that case's behaviour to change, and 'Nobody has said which behaviour the wider case should have' is exactly the situation the skill's three reserved carve-outs exist for. This isn't a taste preference or an unsettled engineering trade-off with no artifact bearing on it (an artifact -- the written cost model -- already settles what the second case should do); it is the delivered code silently overriding that already-declared definition of correct for a case outside the accepted goal. Per the Execution section's rule ('a row's own definition of done that names his eye as the check is describing one of the three cases rule 12/27 already reserve for him -- a taste call, a trade-off no artifact settles, or a change to the definition of correct'), this is the third: closing now would ship a redefinition of correctness for the untouched branch that was never accepted as work and contradicts the written cost model, so the Director holds the checkpoint open and puts the choice (extend the stricter rule to both cases vs. split them apart to preserve the documented note-not-fail behaviour) to the person before closing.
